guard: a pause-plane deadline that elapsed while THIS PROCESS was off the CPU is evidence about the host and not about the effect: the operation is re-entered on the durable pause it already holds, so a `sleep` whose deadline passed during the starvation completes LATE rather than failing; a deadline that elapsed while the loop WAS running is evidence about ONE REPLY and not about the pause either, so it is re-read with bounded exponential backoff and the parked step settles on the answer it was waiting for; the distinction between the two is measured from event-loop lag AND a shortfall in the ticks the window should have contained, so neither a deadline on a running loop nor a wall clock that jumped can be read as starvation; a caller that still cannot be served after a bounded number of consecutive starved attempts fails under L4025 naming its measurement rather than hanging, and one whose plane never answers fails under L4026 naming the plane instead, each bounded on its own count so no interleaving retries forever; and every failure that is not a client deadline is raised on the first attempt, unretried and unwrapped, still recorded as L4000
why: #1508 (2026-09-12). A `sleep("4m")` journalled `failed (L4000)` at load1 118.26 and `ok` at
load1 9.08 with nothing in the program changed. The mechanism is a NATS client deadline, a
`setTimeout`, that cannot run on a blocked loop, so it fires late and rejects `timeout` while
the broker is healthy and its reply is unread in the socket.
MP1 IS THE PRE-FIX CONTROL. It removes exactly the repair, leaving the rest of the tree intact,
and the starvation cell goes red, which is what makes that cell a proof rather than a shape
that would have passed before the change.
MP7 is the band-aid detector, and it exists because the two halves of this repair are each
satisfiable alone: it makes the wrapper retry EVERY failure, which is the fix a lazy reading
would have shipped, and the GENUINE-FAILURE cell reddens on the FIXED tree. A repair that
swallowed all timeouts would pass the starvation half and be caught here.
MP2..MP6 and MP8 take the classifier one branch at a time. The classifier is what separates the
two conditions, so each accepting branch has a mutation whose kill is a REFUSING cell. The
direction a green probe hides a hole in.
MP13/MP14 are a reviewer's finding made permanent. The first draft derived the window from
`Date.now()`, so the SAME reading that inflated the lag inflated `ticksExpected`, and the two
signals were not independent: a +10s step on a healthy loop measured {elapsed 11201, lag 10003,
expected 44, observed 4} and classified `starved`, while a BACKWARD step during a genuine block
classified `fault`, which is #1508's own misattribution returning under an NTP correction. Both
mutations restore exactly that reading, one for the window and one for the tick.
#1619 (2026-09-17) IS THE SECOND HALF, and MP15 IS ITS PRE-FIX CONTROL. A parked `ask` over 7.5
minutes settled `failed (L4000, "timeout")` with 11+ minutes of its deadline unspent, while the
asks under 4.5 minutes settled `ok`. Same client deadline as #1508 and the opposite cause: the
loop was RUNNING and one JetStream reply was simply late, which the classifier answered `fault`,
so the deadline went straight out as the effect's failure. Exposure grew with the step's length
because a parked step issues roughly one 5s plane read per second for its whole duration.
MP16 is #1619's band-aid detector, the mirror of MP7. Retrying a late reply forever is the fix a
lazy reading would have shipped, and a run that hangs on a broker that never answers is neither
alive nor dead; the bound is what makes the re-read a repair instead of a hang.
MP17 keeps the two diagnoses APART. Reporting a late plane as L4025 sends an operator to add
capacity to a host that was never short of it, which is the same class of misattribution both
issues are about, one level up.
